title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 25-32
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 25-32 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Performance stops being about one query and becomes a system-wide budget the moment AI is in the path. This lesson covers latency budgets, the difference between throughput and latency, the batch that makes LLM inference affordable, and the caches that skip work entirely.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Testing Integrations: Mocking, Sandbox Test Strategy, and Integration Test Suites”, a ClaimSubmissionService calls an external clearinghouse. Why can a test not simply call the real endpoint, and what does a mock actually establish?
options: Because callouts in a test are slow but still reach the real service, so mocks only exist to speed the suite up.
Because real callouts are not made in test context, so you implement HttpCalloutMock, register it with Test.setMock, and write one test per response shape so the mock encodes the contract.
Because a mock is a way to make a failing test pass when the vendor API happens to be unavailable.
Because callout logic cannot be covered by tests at all and has to be verified manually before release.
questions.explanation: The platform refuses the network call during a test, so a mock is the specification of the seam: a success shape, an error shape, and a malformed payload each pin down how your code should behave.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Any sandbox will do, because the type only changes how quickly the environment refreshes.
A Developer sandbox is where integration tests against realistic customer data belong, because it refreshes the fastest.
A Partial Copy sandbox is where load and performance testing of an integration path belongs.
Performance and load testing of an integration path belongs only in a Full sandbox, while a Partial Copy sandbox with a template is for integration tests that need realistic data.
questions.explanation: Full is the only replica that supports performance and load testing, and Partial Copy with a sandbox template is how you get realistic data into data-dependent integration tests.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Wrapping the exercise in Test.startTest and Test.stopTest gives that section a fresh set of governor limits and runs queued asynchronous work synchronously at stopTest.
A suite that mocks the external service has verified the seam between the two systems.
Unit tests should read the data they need from the sandbox so the assertions stay realistic.
The Stub API can mock static methods, private methods, properties, and triggers, so any class can be isolated.
questions.explanation: Wrapping the thick part of the test is what lets you assert on a batch job or a callout-heavy path under its own limits, and a mocked suite is a unit test, not an integration test.

questions.question: Per the lesson “General Systems Architecture: Testing AI Systems: Evals, Golden Sets, Canaries, and Regression”, an eval suite is deliberately aimed at problems the agent still fails about half the time. Why can it not answer whether a change broke something?
options: Because LLM-as-a-judge graders are nondeterministic and cannot be calibrated against human graders.
Because the suite runs offline rather than against live production traffic.
Because that is a capability eval, and the regression question needs its own suite with a near-100% expected pass rate.
Because a golden set has to be rebuilt from scratch on every deployment.
questions.explanation: Capability evals are a hill to climb with a low expected pass rate, and a score change on them says nothing about whether an existing behavior regressed.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: A canary that watches only error rate and latency is a software canary wearing an AI costume; hallucination rate, coherence, LLM-as-a-judge results, and business signals belong from the first stage.
Canary routing should be random per turn so the comparison sample stays balanced even mid-conversation.
Because outputs are nondeterministic, canary stages should be shortened so a regression is not masked by soak time.
A golden set of hand-written happy paths is the fastest route to a trustworthy offline score.
questions.explanation: A model can be technically flawless on the infrastructure dashboards and still produce worse reasoning or a tone shift, and nondeterminism means longer soak times rather than shorter ones.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Academic metrics such as perplexity and BLEU score measure task success well enough to be the primary metric.
A golden set has to mirror production traffic patterns, including edge and adversarial cases, and be maintained as production changes.
The eval is the customer, so when the eval and the user disagree you change the model.
Evals should be implemented after the agent ships, once real usage data is available.
questions.explanation: A dataset that does not faithfully reproduce production traffic is a biased design, and an eval is a proxy for the customer, so a disagreement is fixed in the eval.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Apex Architecture: Service Layer, Domain, and Selector Patterns”, a lending org needs a runCreditChecks operation callable from a Lightning component, a batch job, and a REST endpoint, while the credit scoring math belongs to the Account object. Where does each piece live?
options: The service layer exposes runCreditChecks as one method per process that every entry point calls, and the scoring math lives in an Accounts domain class.
The trigger owns runCreditChecks, because a trigger is the only place the platform guarantees the logic runs for every caller.
The selector class owns runCreditChecks, since it already owns everything that queries the Account object.
The batch class owns runCreditChecks, and the Lightning component and REST endpoint call that batch class directly.
questions.explanation: The service layer is the entry point for business processes, so every external caller invokes one service method, and object behavior belongs in the domain class rather than in the entry points.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: A data load that inserts 10,000 accounts is safe as long as the domain logic queries once per account, because triggers run once per record.
Because a batch class and a REST endpoint cannot call into a trigger, the same business rule should be re-implemented inside each entry point.

Because triggers fire in bulk, per-record work such as one query per account blows the governor budget, so the selector takes set-based criteria and the domain handles the whole collection in one pass.
Queries should stay inline near the code that needs them, since a selector class adds a layer without reducing the number of queries a transaction issues.
questions.explanation: Triggers are bulk by default, so a query per record spends the shared governor budget in proportion to batch size; a selector that accepts a collection and queries once is what keeps the domain logic safe.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Full service, domain, and selector stacks should be applied to every org, including small data-centric apps that could be delivered declaratively.
When a requirement changes, a correctly layered solution touches one class, because every SOQL statement lives in the selector, every object rule in the domain, and every process in the service.
A service method should contain the query, the calculation, and the DML inline so a reviewer can read the whole process in one place.
Triggers are the right home for nontrivial logic because they cannot inherit, which keeps the logic close to the record change.
questions.explanation: Separation of concerns is the payoff: the service orchestrates, the domain owns behavior, and the selector owns queries, so a changed rule or a changed schema touches exactly one class.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Flow Architecture: Flow vs Apex vs External Automation, Decision Framework”, a custom object carries 8,000-record Bulk API loads, fires 40 automations on save, and its updates cascade five levels deep with a real recursion risk. Which architectural standard fits?
options: An Apex trigger behind a metadata framework, because bulk handling and recursion control have to be explicit at high density.
A Record-Triggered Flow, because Flow bulkifies and retries automatically and therefore needs no recursion control.
One large flow with entry conditions on every branch, because a single flow is easier to govern than several.
Both a Record-Triggered Flow and an Apex trigger, one per concern, so each mechanism carries half the load.
questions.explanation: Automation density is measured by automation count, data volume, and dependency sprawl, and only Apex gives a developer explicit control over bulk handling and recursion on a dense object.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Flow should be avoided for record-triggered automation because it cannot bulkify or retry on its own.
An object should use a Flow for some rules and a trigger for others, so each mechanism does what it is best at.
Medium density is a hybrid: keep the Record-Triggered Flow as the orchestration layer and move the Map-based, bulk-safe compute into invocable Apex that the Flow calls.
Medium density means migrating straight to Apex, because a Flow plus Apex hybrid creates two entry points on the object.
questions.explanation: The hybrid keeps one readable, ordered entry point in Flow while the pieces Flow cannot express well, such as keyed computes and bulk-safe collection handling, move behind an invocable Apex seam.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Flow is the right tool for a process that must roll back cleanly or commit partially on a boundary condition.
Transactional control makes a process an Apex problem, because Flow has no access to Database.savepoint or Database.rollback.
Flow and Apex express transactional control equally well, so the choice comes down to developer preference.
When a process coordinates an ERP, a WMS, and finance, the orchestration belongs in a trigger so the handoff stays inside Salesforce.
questions.explanation: A savepoint and rollback requirement is an Apex requirement, not a Flow shortcoming to work around, and cross-system orchestration belongs in the external layer that owns those systems.
